example_sentence: We spent the whole day at the beach.

example_translation.es: Pasamos todo el día en la playa.
example_translation.de: Wir verbrachten den ganzen Tag am Strand.
example_translation.fr: Nous avons passé toute la journée à la plage.
example_translation.pt: Passamos o dia inteiro na praia.
example_translation.it: Abbiamo passato tutta la giornata in spiaggia.
example_translation.ru: Мы провели весь день на пляже.
example_translation.ja: 一日中ビーチで過ごしました。
example_translation.zh: 我们在海滩待了一整天。

culturalContext: Beach culture is enormous in English-speaking countries — from California surf culture to Australian beach life. 'Beach body' and 'beach read' are cultural concepts.
usageNotes: 'At/on the beach.' 'Beach' as adjective: 'beach party,' 'beach volleyball.' 'Beachgoer' = person at the beach. 'Beach bum' = someone who hangs out at the beach.
funFact: Australia has over 10,000 beaches — if you visited a new beach every day, it would take you over 27 years to see them all.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Preposition: 'at the beach' or 'on the beach.' Many compound nouns: beachside, beachfront, beach towel.
sentencePatterns: We spent the day at the beach.
commonMistakes: 'On the beach' vs 'at the beach' — 'on' suggests being physically on the sand, 'at' is more general
Confusing 'beach' with 'beech' (a type of tree)
realWorldExamples: The Beach Boys: 'Surfin' USA'
Baywatch — iconic beach TV show
Leonardo DiCaprio in 'The Beach' (2000)

example_sentence: I want to visit Japan next year.

example_translation.es: Quiero visitar Japón el próximo año.
example_translation.tr: Gelecek yıl Japonya'yı ziyaret etmek istiyorum.
example_translation.de: Ich möchte nächstes Jahr Japan besuchen.
example_translation.fr: Je veux visiter le Japon l'année prochaine.
example_translation.pt: Quero visitar o Japão no próximo ano.
example_translation.it: Voglio visitare il Giappone l'anno prossimo.
example_translation.ru: Я хочу посетить Японию в следующем году.
example_translation.ja: 来年日本を訪問したいです。
example_translation.zh: 我想明年去日本旅游。

culturalContext: Visiting places and people is a core English social activity. 'Visit' carries warmth: 'Come visit us!' reflects hospitality in English-speaking cultures.
usageNotes: 'Visit' + person (no preposition): 'visit my grandmother.' 'Visit' + place: 'visit Paris.' BrE: 'pay a visit.' Noun: 'a visit.'
funFact: The most visited English-speaking city is London, with approximately 20 million international visitors per year.
grammarNote: Transitive verb (no preposition needed): 'visit someone/somewhere.' Also a noun: 'a visit.' 'Visitor' = person who visits.
commonMistakes: Adding unnecessary preposition: 'visit to London' is a noun phrase, but 'visit London' is the verb usage (no 'to')
Confusing 'visit' with 'attend' (visit = go to see, attend = be present at an event)
realWorldExamples: Tourism ads: 'Visit [country]!'
When Harry Met Sally: visiting scenes
Charlie and the Chocolate Factory: visiting the factory

example_sentence: I work in a small office downtown.

example_translation.es: Trabajo en una pequeña oficina en el centro.
example_translation.tr: Şehir merkezinde küçük bir ofiste çalışıyorum.
example_translation.de: Ich arbeite in einem kleinen Büro in der Innenstadt.
example_translation.fr: Je travaille dans un petit bureau au centre-ville.
example_translation.pt: Trabalho em um pequeno escritório no centro.
example_translation.it: Lavoro in un piccolo ufficio in centro.
example_translation.ru: Я работаю в небольшом офисе в центре города.
example_translation.ja: ダウンタウンの小さなオフィスで働いています。
example_translation.zh: 我在市中心的一个小办公室工作。

culturalContext: Office culture dominates English-speaking work life. 'The Office' (TV show) satirized workplace dynamics and became a global cultural phenomenon.
usageNotes: 'At the office' or 'in the office.' 'Office' as adjective: 'office hours,' 'office supplies.' 'Home office' gained huge usage post-2020.
funFact: 'The Office' (US version, 2005-2013) is the most-streamed TV show in history, with billions of minutes watched annually.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Preposition: 'at/in the office.' Compounds: office building, office hours, box office, post office.
commonMistakes: 'In the office' (inside) vs 'at the office' (general location) — subtle difference
Not knowing 'box office' means ticket sales/cinema ticket area
realWorldExamples: The Office — iconic TV show
Office Space (1999): 'I believe you have my stapler.'
Post-2020: 'home office' and 'return to office' debates

example_sentence: The meeting starts at ten o'clock.

example_translation.es: La reunión empieza a las diez.
example_translation.de: Die Besprechung beginnt um zehn Uhr.
example_translation.fr: La réunion commence à dix heures.
example_translation.pt: A reunião começa às dez horas.
example_translation.it: La riunione inizia alle dieci.
example_translation.ja: 会議は10時に始まります。
example_translation.zh: 会议十点开始。

culturalContext: Meeting culture is central to English-speaking corporate life. 'This could have been an email' is a famous complaint about unnecessary meetings.
usageNotes: 'Have/hold a meeting.' 'Meeting' also means encounter: 'a chance meeting.' 'Board meeting,' 'staff meeting,' 'town hall meeting.'
funFact: The average American office worker spends about 31 hours per month in unproductive meetings, costing companies billions annually.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Gerund of 'meet.' 'Meeting' as noun needs article: 'a meeting,' 'the meeting.' Compounds: meeting room, meeting point.
commonMistakes: Confusing 'meet' (verb) with 'meeting' (noun) in structure
'I have meeting' (wrong — 'I have a meeting')
realWorldExamples: Corporate meme: 'This meeting could have been an email.'
Zoom meeting culture post-2020
The Apprentice: 'You're in the boardroom meeting.'

example_sentence: She found a new job last month.

example_translation.es: Ella encontró un nuevo empleo el mes pasado.
example_translation.tr: Geçen ay yeni bir iş buldu.
example_translation.de: Sie hat letzten Monat einen neuen Job gefunden.
example_translation.fr: Elle a trouvé un nouvel emploi le mois dernier.
example_translation.pt: Ela encontrou um novo emprego no mês passado.
example_translation.it: Ha trovato un nuovo lavoro il mese scorso.
example_translation.ru: Она нашла новую работу в прошлом месяце.
example_translation.ja: 彼女は先月新しい仕事を見つけました。
example_translation.zh: 她上个月找到了一份新工作。

culturalContext: 'Job' is central to identity in English-speaking cultures. 'What do you do?' is one of the first questions asked when meeting someone new.
usageNotes: 'Job' (countable, specific position) vs 'work' (uncountable, general activity). 'Get a job,' 'lose a job.' 'Job' also = task: 'Good job!'
funFact: In English-speaking cultures, asking 'What do you do?' (meaning your job) within minutes of meeting someone is standard — in many other cultures, this is considered rude.
grammarNote: Countable noun. 'A job' (specific) vs 'work' (general, uncountable). 'Job' also means task: 'You did a great job!'
commonMistakes: Confusing 'job' (countable) with 'work' (uncountable): 'I'm looking for a work' (wrong — 'work' or 'a job')
'Job' as compliment: 'Good job!' (AmE) is very common
realWorldExamples: Steve Jobs — tech icon whose surname means 'occupations'
The Pursuit of Happyness: job-hunting story
Common praise: 'Great job!'

example_sentence: My boss is very understanding.

example_translation.es: Mi jefe es muy comprensivo.
example_translation.de: Mein Chef ist sehr verständnisvoll.
example_translation.fr: Mon patron est très compréhensif.
example_translation.pt: Meu chefe é muito compreensivo.
example_translation.it: Il mio capo è molto comprensivo.
example_translation.ja: 上司はとても理解があります。
example_translation.zh: 我的老板非常通情达理。

culturalContext: 'Boss' has evolved from purely workplace to cultural slang. 'Like a boss' became a viral phrase meaning doing something with supreme confidence.
usageNotes: 'Boss' = supervisor/manager. Slang: 'boss' = excellent/cool. 'Like a boss' = with authority and confidence. 'Boss around' = give orders rudely.
funFact: The Lonely Island's 'Like a Boss' (2009) turned the word into a viral meme, now used to describe any confident action.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Also adjective (slang): 'That's boss!' Also verb: 'to boss someone around.' Plural: bosses.
commonMistakes: Not knowing 'boss' has positive slang meaning
Confusing 'boss' with 'chef' (which means boss in French/German but means cook in English)
realWorldExamples: The Lonely Island: 'Like a Boss'
Bruce Springsteen: 'The Boss' — his nickname
Tony Danza: 'Who's the Boss?' — TV show

example_sentence: She was angry because she missed the bus.

example_translation.es: Estaba enfadada porque perdió el autobús.
example_translation.de: Sie war wütend, weil sie den Bus verpasst hatte.
example_translation.fr: Elle était en colère car elle avait raté le bus.
example_translation.pt: Ela estava zangada porque perdeu o ônibus.
example_translation.it: Era arrabbiata perché aveva perso l'autobus.
example_translation.ru: Она разозлилась, потому что опоздала на автобус.
example_translation.ja: バスに乗り遅れたので怒っていました。
example_translation.zh: 她因为错过了公共汽车而生气。

culturalContext: Expressing anger has specific social rules in English-speaking cultures. Direct expressions of anger are often considered unprofessional or socially unacceptable.
usageNotes: 'Angry' + 'at/with someone' + 'about something.' Gradations: annoyed < irritated < angry < furious < livid. 'Angry' vs 'mad' — 'mad' also means crazy (BrE).
funFact: In British English, saying you're 'cross' is a very mild way to say angry, while in American English, 'cross' as an emotion is barely used.
grammarNote: Adjective. Comparative: angrier. Prepositions: 'angry at/with [person],' 'angry about [thing].' Related: anger (noun), angrily (adverb).
sentencePatterns: She was angry at her boss.
commonMistakes: Preposition: 'angry to someone' (wrong — 'angry with/at')
'Mad' in AmE = angry, in BrE = crazy — confusing cross-dialectally
realWorldExamples: Hulk: 'You won't like me when I'm angry.'
Inside Out: Anger as a character
Taylor Swift: 'Bad Blood' — anger channeled into music

example_sentence: I'm very tired after a long day.

example_translation.es: Estoy muy cansado después de un largo día.
example_translation.tr: Uzun bir günün ardından çok yorgunum.
example_translation.de: Ich bin sehr müde nach einem langen Tag.
example_translation.fr: Je suis très fatigué après une longue journée.
example_translation.pt: Estou muito cansado depois de um dia longo.
example_translation.it: Sono molto stanco dopo una lunga giornata.
example_translation.ru: Я очень устал после долгого дня.
example_translation.ja: 長い一日の後でとても疲れています。
example_translation.zh: 忙了一整天，我很累。

culturalContext: Tiredness and burnout are major topics in English-speaking cultures. 'I'm tired' has become almost a default state in modern English conversation.
usageNotes: 'Tired' = physically or emotionally exhausted. 'Tired of' = bored/fed up with. 'Tiresome' = annoying. Gradations: tired < exhausted < shattered < dead tired.
funFact: The CDC estimates that 1 in 3 American adults don't get enough sleep, making 'I'm tired' perhaps the most relatable English sentence.
grammarNote: Adjective. 'Tired' (general) vs 'tired of' + noun/gerund (fed up). 'Tiring' = causing tiredness. 'Tiresome' = annoying.
commonMistakes: Confusing 'tired' (how you feel) with 'tiring' (causing tiredness)
'Tired of' = fed up, not physically tired
realWorldExamples: Madcon: 'I'm tired of being what you want me to be.'
Fannie Lou Hamer: 'I'm sick and tired of being sick and tired.'
Modern meme culture: 'I'm tired' as a lifestyle

example_sentence: The children are excited about the trip.

example_translation.es: Los niños están emocionados por el viaje.
example_translation.de: Die Kinder sind aufgeregt wegen der Reise.
example_translation.fr: Les enfants sont excités par le voyage.
example_translation.pt: As crianças estão animadas com a viagem.
example_translation.it: I bambini sono emozionati per il viaggio.
example_translation.ja: 子供たちは旅行にワクワクしています。
example_translation.zh: 孩子们对这次旅行很兴奋。

culturalContext: Excitement and enthusiasm are valued in American English culture. 'I'm so excited!' is a common expression that might seem over-the-top to more reserved cultures.
usageNotes: 'Excited about/for something.' 'Exciting' = causing excitement. American English tends to express excitement more openly than British English.
funFact: The Pointer Sisters' 'I'm So Excited' (1984) remains the go-to song for expressing anticipation in English-speaking media.
grammarNote: Adjective. 'Excited' (how you feel) vs 'exciting' (what causes the feeling). Preposition: 'excited about/for.'
commonMistakes: Confusing 'excited' with 'exciting': 'I'm exciting' (wrong for the feeling — 'I'm excited')
'Excited' in some languages has sexual connotations — not in standard English
realWorldExamples: Pointer Sisters: 'I'm So Excited'
Steve Irwin: 'Crikey! I'm excited!'
Apple keynotes: 'We're really excited about this.'

example_sentence: I'm worried about the exam tomorrow.

example_translation.es: Estoy preocupado por el examen de mañana.
example_translation.de: Ich bin besorgt wegen der Prüfung morgen.
example_translation.fr: Je suis inquiet pour l'examen de demain.
example_translation.pt: Estou preocupado com a prova de amanhã.
example_translation.it: Sono preoccupato per l'esame di domani.
example_translation.ja: 明日の試験が心配です。
example_translation.zh: 我担心明天的考试。

culturalContext: Worry and anxiety are increasingly discussed in English-speaking mental health awareness movements. 'Don't worry, be happy' represents the cultural ideal.
usageNotes: 'Worried about' + noun/gerund. 'Don't worry' = common reassurance. 'Worry' as noun: 'no worries' (AusE/informal). 'Worrisome' = causing worry.
funFact: 'No worries' originated in Australian English and has spread globally, now used commonly in American and British English.
grammarNote: Adjective. 'Worried about' + noun/gerund. 'Worry' also a verb and noun. 'Worrying' = adjective or gerund.
commonMistakes: Preposition: 'worried for' (less common) vs 'worried about' (standard)
Confusing 'worried' (feeling) with 'worrying' (causing worry)
realWorldExamples: Bobby McFerrin: 'Don't Worry, Be Happy'
Australian English: 'No worries, mate!'
Common text: 'No worries' = casual 'you're welcome'

example_sentence: We climbed the mountain last weekend.

example_translation.es: Subimos la montaña el fin de semana pasado.
example_translation.de: Wir haben letztes Wochenende den Berg bestiegen.
example_translation.fr: Nous avons escaladé la montagne le week-end dernier.
example_translation.pt: Escalamos a montanha no fim de semana passado.
example_translation.it: Abbiamo scalato la montagna lo scorso fine settimana.
example_translation.ru: Мы поднялись на гору в прошлые выходные.
example_translation.ja: 先週末に山に登りました。
example_translation.zh: 我们上周末爬了山。

culturalContext: Mountains symbolize challenge and achievement in English: 'move mountains,' 'mountain of work,' 'mountain to climb.' Mountain climbing culture is significant.
usageNotes: 'Mountain' for large elevations, 'hill' for smaller ones. 'Make a mountain out of a molehill' = exaggerate. 'Mountain range' = group of mountains.
funFact: Edmund Hillary, a New Zealander, was the first confirmed person to reach the summit of Mount Everest in 1953, saying 'We knocked the bastard off!'
grammarNote: Countable noun. Capitalize when part of a name: 'Mount Everest.' 'Mountain' as adjective: 'mountain bike,' 'mountain lion.'
sentencePatterns: Don't make a mountain out of a molehill.
commonMistakes: Confusing 'mount' (title: Mount Everest) with 'mountain' (general noun)
'Mountain of' + uncountable noun for emphasis: 'a mountain of work'
realWorldExamples: Joe Cocker: 'You Can Leave Your Hat On' — mountain climbing
The Lord of the Rings: Mount Doom
Sound of Music: 'Climb Every Mountain'

example_sentence: The river flows through the city.

example_translation.es: El río fluye a través de la ciudad.
example_translation.de: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
example_translation.fr: La rivière traverse la ville.
example_translation.pt: O rio passa pela cidade.
example_translation.it: Il fiume scorre attraverso la città.
example_translation.ja: 川が街の中を流れています。
example_translation.zh: 河流穿过城市。

culturalContext: Rivers have historical and cultural significance in English. 'Selling down the river' (betrayal) has origins in American slavery history.
usageNotes: 'The River [Name]' (BrE: 'the River Thames') or '[Name] River' (AmE: 'the Mississippi River'). 'Down the river' = betrayed.
funFact: In British English, the river name comes after 'River' (River Thames), while in American English it comes before (Mississippi River).
grammarNote: Countable noun. Always with 'the': 'the river.' BrE: 'the River Thames.' AmE: 'the Mississippi River.' Figurative: 'a river of tears.'
sentencePatterns: The river flows into the sea.
commonMistakes: Naming convention: 'River Thames' (BrE) vs 'Colorado River' (AmE)
Omitting 'the': 'I went to river' (wrong — 'the river')
realWorldExamples: Springsteen: 'The River'
Mark Twain's Mississippi River stories
Three Doors Down: 'Cry Me a River' — also Justin Timberlake

example_sentence: She gave me a beautiful flower.

example_translation.es: Ella me dio una hermosa flor.
example_translation.de: Sie gab mir eine schöne Blume.
example_translation.fr: Elle m'a donné une belle fleur.
example_translation.pt: Ela me deu uma bela flor.
example_translation.it: Mi ha dato un bel fiore.
example_translation.ja: 彼女は私に美しい花をくれました。
example_translation.zh: 她给了我一朵美丽的花。

culturalContext: Flowers carry symbolic meanings in English culture: roses (love), lilies (purity), poppies (remembrance of war dead). Giving flowers is a key social gesture.
usageNotes: 'Flower' countable. 'In flower/bloom' = flowering. 'Flowery' = ornate (can be negative for writing). 'Flower power' = 1960s peace movement.
funFact: Red roses became the ultimate symbol of romantic love thanks to Victorian 'floriography' — the language of flowers.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Plural: flowers. Also a verb: 'The plant flowered.' 'Flowery' = adjective (ornate, overly decorative).
commonMistakes: Confusing 'flour' (baking) with 'flower' (plant) — homophones
'Flowery language' = overly elaborate (negative connotation)
realWorldExamples: Miley Cyrus: 'Flowers'
Valentine's Day: red roses tradition
Poppy Day: remembering fallen soldiers (UK/Commonwealth)

example_sentence: He stayed home because he was sick.

example_translation.es: Se quedó en casa porque estaba enfermo.
example_translation.de: Er blieb zu Hause, weil er krank war.
example_translation.fr: Il est resté à la maison car il était malade.
example_translation.pt: Ele ficou em casa porque estava doente.
example_translation.it: È rimasto a casa perché era malato.
example_translation.ru: Он остался дома, потому что болел.
example_translation.ja: 病気だったので家にいました。
example_translation.zh: 他因为生病了所以待在家里。

culturalContext: Being sick carries different social implications across English cultures. In AmE, 'calling in sick' is standard. In the UK, 'pulling a sickie' means faking illness.
usageNotes: 'Sick' in AmE = ill. 'Sick' in BrE can specifically mean nauseous ('I feel sick'). Slang: 'sick' = amazing/cool (young people). 'Sick of' = tired of.
funFact: British slang inverted 'sick' to mean 'amazing' around 2010, following the same pattern as 'wicked' and 'bad' becoming positive.
grammarNote: Adjective. Multiple meanings: ill (AmE), nauseous (BrE), amazing (slang). 'Sick of' = fed up with. 'Sickness' = noun.
commonMistakes: BrE/AmE difference: 'sick' in BrE specifically means nauseous
Not knowing youth slang: 'That's sick!' = 'That's awesome!'
realWorldExamples: Ferris Bueller's Day Off: faking being sick
Destiny's Child: 'I'm not gon' call in sick'
British slang: 'That trick was sick, mate!'

example_sentence: She works at the city hospital.

example_translation.es: Ella trabaja en el hospital de la ciudad.
example_translation.de: Sie arbeitet im Stadtkrankenhaus.
example_translation.fr: Elle travaille à l'hôpital de la ville.
example_translation.pt: Ela trabalha no hospital da cidade.
example_translation.it: Lavora all'ospedale della città.
example_translation.ja: 彼女は市の病院で働いています。
example_translation.zh: 她在市医院工作。

culturalContext: Hospitals are central institutions in English-speaking countries. Healthcare debates (especially in the US vs UK NHS system) are major cultural conversations.
usageNotes: 'In hospital' (BrE, no article) vs 'in the hospital' (AmE, with article). 'Hospital' as adjective: 'hospital bed,' 'hospital gown.'
funFact: The UK's National Health Service (NHS) is free at point of use, while US hospital bills are the #1 cause of personal bankruptcy.
grammarNote: Countable noun. BrE: 'in hospital' (no article). AmE: 'in the hospital.' Compounds: hospital ward, hospital bed.
commonMistakes: Article difference: 'in hospital' (BrE) vs 'in the hospital' (AmE)
Pronunciation: the 'h' is pronounced — not silent
realWorldExamples: Grey's Anatomy: Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital
ER — classic hospital drama
NHS: the UK's beloved healthcare system

example_sentence: Take this medicine three times a day.

example_translation.es: Toma esta medicina tres veces al día.
example_translation.tr: Bu ilacı günde üç kez al.
example_translation.de: Nimm diese Medizin dreimal am Tag.
example_translation.fr: Prends ce médicament trois fois par jour.
example_translation.pt: Tome este remédio três vezes ao dia.
example_translation.it: Prendi questa medicina tre volte al giorno.
example_translation.ru: Принимайте это лекарство три раза в день.
example_translation.ja: この薬を1日3回飲んでください。
example_translation.ko: 이 약을 하루에 세 번 드세요.
example_translation.zh: 每天吃三次这种药。

culturalContext: Medicine represents both healthcare and the medical profession in English. 'Take your medicine' can be literal or figurative (face consequences).
usageNotes: Uncountable (general field) or countable (specific medication). 'Take medicine' (not 'eat medicine'). 'Medicine' = the profession or the substance.
funFact: The phrase 'laughter is the best medicine' dates back to biblical Proverbs and remains one of the most quoted health sayings in English.
grammarNote: Uncountable (field/substance) or countable (types). 'Take medicine' (not 'eat' or 'drink'). 'Medical' = adjective.
commonMistakes: 'Eat medicine' (wrong — 'take medicine')
Confusing 'medicine' (substance/field) with 'medical' (adjective)
realWorldExamples: Bon Jovi: 'Bad Medicine'
Dr. House: 'It's not lupus' — medical drama
Proverb: 'Laughter is the best medicine.'

example_sentence: I use a computer for my work.

example_translation.es: Uso una computadora para mi trabajo.
example_translation.de: Ich benutze einen Computer für meine Arbeit.
example_translation.fr: J'utilise un ordinateur pour mon travail.
example_translation.pt: Uso um computador para meu trabalho.
example_translation.it: Uso un computer per il mio lavoro.
example_translation.ja: 仕事にコンピュータを使っています。
example_translation.zh: 我用电脑工作。

culturalContext: Computers have transformed English with new vocabulary: 'crash,' 'bug,' 'virus,' 'cloud' — all gained new meanings. Digital literacy is a key cultural value.
usageNotes: 'Computer' countable. 'Desktop/laptop/tablet.' 'On the computer' (using it). 'Computer science' = academic field. 'Computer' as adjective: 'computer-generated.'
funFact: The first computers were actually people — 'computer' was a job title for humans who performed calculations, predominantly women during WWII.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Compounds: computer science, computer program, personal computer (PC). Adjective use: 'computer-generated.'
sentencePatterns: I work on a computer all day.
commonMistakes: 'In the computer' vs 'on the computer' — 'on' for using, 'in' for stored data
Plural: 'I'm good with computer' (wrong — 'computers')
realWorldExamples: Apple: 'Think Different' — personal computer revolution
2001: A Space Odyssey: 'HAL' computer
The Social Network: 'The Facebook was built on a computer in a dorm room.'

example_sentence: The internet connection is very slow today.

example_translation.es: La conexión a internet está muy lenta hoy.
example_translation.de: Die Internetverbindung ist heute sehr langsam.
example_translation.fr: La connexion internet est très lente aujourd'hui.
example_translation.pt: A conexão com a internet está muito lenta hoje.
example_translation.it: La connessione internet è molto lenta oggi.
example_translation.ja: 今日はインターネット接続がとても遅いです。
example_translation.zh: 今天网速很慢。

culturalContext: The internet has fundamentally changed English culture, communication, and language itself. Internet culture has created entirely new words and communication styles.
usageNotes: 'The internet' (with 'the'). 'Online' = on the internet. 'Wi-Fi' = wireless internet. Capitalization: traditionally 'Internet' (proper noun), now often 'internet.'
funFact: The first message ever sent on the internet (1969) was 'LO' — it was supposed to be 'LOGIN' but the system crashed after two letters.
grammarNote: Usually uncountable with 'the': 'the internet.' 'Online' = adjective/adverb. Previously capitalized as proper noun; now often lowercase.
sentencePatterns: I found it on the internet.
commonMistakes: Capitalization debate: 'Internet' vs 'internet' (both acceptable now)
Article: 'on internet' (wrong — 'on the internet')
realWorldExamples: The IT Crowd: 'The internet — it's not a truck, it's a series of tubes.'
Tim Berners-Lee: inventor of the World Wide Web
Bo Burnham: 'Welcome to the Internet'

example_sentence: She is a university student.

example_translation.es: Ella es una estudiante universitaria.
example_translation.de: Sie ist eine Universitätsstudentin.
example_translation.fr: Elle est une étudiante universitaire.
example_translation.pt: Ela é uma estudante universitária.
example_translation.it: È una studentessa universitaria.
example_translation.ja: 彼女は大学生です。
example_translation.zh: 她是一名大学生。

culturalContext: Student life is a significant cultural phase in English-speaking countries. University/college culture (especially in the US) is a major identity-forming experience.
usageNotes: 'Student' for all levels (K-12 and university). 'Pupil' in BrE for younger students. 'Student' as adjective: 'student loan,' 'student visa,' 'student life.'
funFact: Student loan debt in the US exceeds $1.7 trillion, making 'student debt' one of the most discussed financial topics in American English.
grammarNote: Countable noun. 'Student' as adjective: student council, student body, student housing. 'Studious' = adjective meaning diligent.
commonMistakes: BrE: 'pupil' for school, 'student' for university — AmE uses 'student' for all levels
Confusing 'student' with 'learner' (student = enrolled, learner = anyone learning)
realWorldExamples: Animal House (1978) — student life comedy
Student protests: historically significant in English-speaking countries
Grease: 'Back to school' student culture

example_sentence: Let's watch a movie tonight.

example_translation.es: Veamos una película esta noche.
example_translation.de: Lass uns heute Abend einen Film anschauen.
example_translation.fr: Regardons un film ce soir.
example_translation.pt: Vamos assistir a um filme hoje à noite.
example_translation.it: Guardiamo un film stasera.
example_translation.ja: 今夜映画を観ましょう。
example_translation.zh: 今晚我们看电影吧。

culturalContext: Movie culture is central to English-speaking entertainment. Hollywood dominates global cinema, and 'movie night' is a staple social activity.
usageNotes: AmE: 'movie.' BrE: 'film.' 'Go to the movies' (AmE) = 'go to the cinema' (BrE). 'Movie star,' 'movie theater' (AmE) = 'film star,' 'cinema' (BrE).
funFact: Hollywood produces about 700 movies per year, but Bollywood (India) produces over 1,500 — though Hollywood dominates English-language cinema.
grammarNote: Countable noun. AmE 'movie' = BrE 'film.' Plural: movies. Compounds: movie star, movie theater, movie night.
commonMistakes: AmE/BrE: 'movie' vs 'film' — 'film' sounds more formal/artistic in AmE
'Go to the movies' (AmE) vs 'go to the cinema' (BrE)
realWorldExamples: The Oscars — Academy Awards for best movies
IMDB: Internet Movie Database
Movie quotes: a fundamental part of English pop culture

example_sentence: I need to buy some groceries.

example_translation.es: Necesito comprar algunas provisiones.
example_translation.de: Ich muss ein paar Lebensmittel kaufen.
example_translation.fr: Je dois acheter des courses.
example_translation.pt: Preciso comprar algumas compras.
example_translation.it: Devo comprare della spesa.
example_translation.ja: 食料品を買う必要があります。
example_translation.zh: 我需要买一些杂货。

culturalContext: Consumer culture is significant in English-speaking countries. 'Buy' connects to shopping culture, Black Friday, and the concept of 'retail therapy.'
usageNotes: Irregular: buy-bought-bought. 'Buy into' = believe/invest. 'Buy time' = delay. 'Buy someone a drink' = treat someone.
funFact: Americans spend an average of $5,400 per year on impulse purchases — the concept of 'impulse buying' is a major English-language marketing topic.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: buy-bought-bought. 'Buy' + person + thing (double object): 'Buy me a coffee.' 'Buy into' = believe in or invest.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'buyed' (wrong — 'bought')
Confusing 'buy' and 'by' and 'bye' — homophones
realWorldExamples: Black Friday: biggest buying day
Amazon: 'Buy Now with 1-Click'
Common expression: 'I don't buy it' = I don't believe it

example_sentence: They sell fresh vegetables at the market.

example_translation.es: Venden verduras frescas en el mercado.
example_translation.de: Sie verkaufen frisches Gemüse auf dem Markt.
example_translation.fr: Ils vendent des légumes frais au marché.
example_translation.pt: Eles vendem legumes frescos no mercado.
example_translation.it: Vendono verdure fresche al mercato.
example_translation.ru: Они продают свежие овощи на рынке.
example_translation.ja: 市場で新鮮な野菜を売っています。
example_translation.zh: 他们在市场上卖新鲜蔬菜。

culturalContext: 'Sell' is central to business English and entrepreneurial culture. 'Selling yourself' in interviews and the 'sales pitch' are essential professional skills.
usageNotes: Irregular: sell-sold-sold. 'Sell out' = betray principles or sell all tickets. 'Hard sell' = aggressive selling. 'Sell yourself short' = undervalue yourself.
funFact: The concept of 'selling yourself' in a job interview is an English-language cultural norm that many international candidates find uncomfortable.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: sell-sold-sold. 'Sell' can take double object: 'sell someone something.' 'Sell out' = phrasal verb with multiple meanings.
sentencePatterns: We need to sell more products.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'selled' (wrong — 'sold')
Confusing 'sell' with 'sale' (sell = verb, sale = noun)
realWorldExamples: Shark Tank: entrepreneurs selling ideas
'Sell out' — used in music to mean abandoning artistic integrity
Jordan Belfort (Wolf of Wall Street): 'Sell me this pen.'

example_sentence: Can I pay by credit card?

example_translation.es: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta de crédito?
example_translation.de: Kann ich mit Kreditkarte bezahlen?
example_translation.fr: Puis-je payer par carte de crédit ?
example_translation.pt: Posso pagar com cartão de crédito?
example_translation.it: Posso pagare con carta di credito?
example_translation.ru: Могу ли я заплатить кредитной картой?
example_translation.ja: クレジットカードで支払えますか？
example_translation.zh: 我可以用信用卡付款吗？

culturalContext: Payment culture is evolving rapidly in English-speaking countries. From 'pay cash' to 'pay by card' to 'Apple Pay,' the concept of paying is constantly in flux.
usageNotes: Irregular: pay-paid-paid. 'Pay for' + item/service. 'Pay attention' = focus. 'Pay a visit' = visit. 'Pay off' = repay fully or yield results.
funFact: Sweden is becoming the world's first cashless society, but the English phrase 'cash is king' still persists in business contexts.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: pay-paid-paid. 'Pay for' (item). 'Pay' (person). 'Pay off' = repay or succeed. 'Pay' also a noun: 'good pay.'
sentencePatterns: How would you like to pay?
I need to pay the bill.
It will pay off in the end.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'payed' (wrong in most contexts — 'paid')
'Pay attention to' (not 'pay attention at')
realWorldExamples: NSYNC: 'Bye Bye Bye' — emotional payment theme
Apple Pay, Google Pay — mobile payments
Common expression: 'Crime doesn't pay.'

example_sentence: Please wait here for a moment.

example_translation.es: Por favor espera aquí un momento.
example_translation.de: Bitte warte hier einen Moment.
example_translation.fr: Veuillez attendre ici un moment.
example_translation.pt: Por favor, espere aqui um momento.
example_translation.it: Per favore aspetta qui un momento.
example_translation.ja: ここで少々お待ちください。
example_translation.zh: 请在这里等一下。

culturalContext: Patience and waiting are valued differently across English-speaking cultures. 'Good things come to those who wait' vs the American 'time is money' create tension.
usageNotes: 'Wait for' + person/thing. 'Wait on' = serve (AmE) or wait for (AmE informal). 'Can't wait' = very excited. 'Wait and see' = be patient.
funFact: The average person spends approximately 6 months of their lifetime waiting in queues (lines), according to a British study.
grammarNote: Regular verb: wait-waited-waited. 'Wait for' (person/thing). Intransitive (no direct object). 'Can't wait to' = very excited to.
commonMistakes: 'Wait' vs 'expect': 'wait' = physical waiting, 'expect' = anticipate
Omitting 'for': 'wait me' (wrong — 'wait for me')
realWorldExamples: Tom Petty: 'The Waiting is the hardest part.'
Common meme: 'Still waiting...'
Heinz ketchup ad: 'Good things come to those who wait.'

example_sentence: I remember my first day at school.

example_translation.es: Recuerdo mi primer día en la escuela.
example_translation.de: Ich erinnere mich an meinen ersten Schultag.
example_translation.fr: Je me souviens de mon premier jour d'école.
example_translation.pt: Lembro do meu primeiro dia na escola.
example_translation.it: Ricordo il mio primo giorno di scuola.
example_translation.ru: Я помню свой первый день в школе.
example_translation.ja: 学校の初日を覚えています。
example_translation.zh: 我记得上学的第一天。

culturalContext: Memory and remembrance are important in English culture. 'Remember' connects to memorials, nostalgia, and the cultural value of honoring the past.
usageNotes: 'Remember + gerund' = recall a past event. 'Remember + to-infinitive' = don't forget to do something. 'Remember me to [someone]' = send regards (formal).
funFact: The phrase 'Remember, remember, the 5th of November' (Guy Fawkes Night) is one of the most famous English memory rhymes.
grammarNote: Regular verb. Critical distinction: 'remember doing' (recall past) vs 'remember to do' (don't forget future). Also noun: 'remembrance.'
commonMistakes: 'Remember doing' (past memory) vs 'remember to do' (future obligation) — critical difference
Confusing 'remember' with 'remind': 'Remind me' (someone else triggers memory)
realWorldExamples: The Lion King: 'Remember who you are.'
Guy Fawkes: 'Remember, remember, the 5th of November.'
Coco (Pixar): 'Remember Me'

example_sentence: Don't forget to lock the door.

example_translation.es: No olvides cerrar la puerta con llave.
example_translation.de: Vergiss nicht, die Tür abzuschließen.
example_translation.fr: N'oublie pas de fermer la porte à clé.
example_translation.pt: Não esqueça de trancar a porta.
example_translation.it: Non dimenticare di chiudere la porta a chiave.
example_translation.ja: ドアに鍵をかけるのを忘れないで。
example_translation.zh: 别忘了锁门。

culturalContext: Forgetting is treated with humor and concern in English culture. 'Senior moments,' 'brain fog,' and forgetting names are common English conversation topics.
usageNotes: Irregular: forget-forgot-forgotten. 'Forget about it' = don't worry (also 'fuhgeddaboudit' in NYC Italian-American slang). 'Forget + gerund' = lose memory of. 'Forget + infinitive' = fail to remember to do.
funFact: 'Fuhgeddaboudit' (forget about it) in New York Italian-American dialect can mean yes, no, you're welcome, or an expression of amazement — depending on context.
grammarNote: Irregular: forget-forgot-forgotten. 'Forget doing' (lost memory) vs 'forget to do' (failed to do). 'Forgetful' = adjective.
commonMistakes: 'Forget doing' vs 'forget to do' — same distinction as 'remember'
Past participle: 'I have forgot' (informal) vs 'I have forgotten' (standard)
realWorldExamples: Donnie Brasco: 'Fuhgeddaboudit!'
Finding Nemo: Dory — 'I suffer from short-term memory loss.'
Gotye: 'Somebody That I Used to Know' — about forgetting

example_sentence: I think this is a great idea.

example_translation.es: Creo que es una gran idea.
example_translation.de: Ich denke, das ist eine großartige Idee.
example_translation.fr: Je pense que c'est une excellente idée.
example_translation.pt: Acho que é uma ótima ideia.
example_translation.it: Penso che sia un'ottima idea.
example_translation.ja: これは素晴らしいアイデアだと思います。
example_translation.zh: 我认为这是一个很好的主意。

culturalContext: Thinking and critical thought are highly valued in English-speaking education systems. 'Think different' (Apple), 'think outside the box' — creativity in thought is prized.
usageNotes: Irregular: think-thought-thought. 'Think about' = consider. 'Think of' = have an idea/recall. 'I think so' = agreement/belief. 'Think over' = consider carefully.
funFact: Rodin's famous sculpture 'The Thinker' has become the universal English-language symbol for deep thought and contemplation.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: think-thought-thought. 'Think about' (consider), 'think of' (imagine/recall). 'Thinking' as noun: 'critical thinking.'
commonMistakes: 'Think about' vs 'think of' — subtle difference (about = consider, of = imagine/recall)
Past tense: 'thinked' (wrong — 'thought')
realWorldExamples: Apple: 'Think Different'
Rodin: 'The Thinker' sculpture
Winnie the Pooh: 'Think, think, think!'

example_sentence: Do you know where the station is?

example_translation.es: ¿Sabes dónde está la estación?
example_translation.de: Weißt du, wo der Bahnhof ist?
example_translation.fr: Sais-tu où est la gare ?
example_translation.pt: Você sabe onde fica a estação?
example_translation.it: Sai dov'è la stazione?
example_translation.ja: 駅がどこか知っていますか？
example_translation.zh: 你知道车站在哪里吗？

culturalContext: 'Knowledge is power' (Francis Bacon) is a foundational English-language concept. Knowing vs not knowing carries social implications — 'in the know' means being informed.
usageNotes: Irregular: know-knew-known. 'Know' vs 'meet' for first encounters (BrE: 'Do you know John?' can mean 'Have you met?'). 'You know' = filler phrase in speech.
funFact: 'You know' is one of the most overused filler phrases in English — some speakers say it 40+ times in a single conversation.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: know-knew-known. No continuous form for knowledge state: 'I know' (not 'I am knowing'). 'Know how to' + verb.
commonMistakes: Using continuous: 'I am knowing' (wrong — 'I know')
Confusing 'know' and 'no' — homophones
realWorldExamples: Jon Snow: 'You know nothing, Jon Snow.'
Socrates: 'I know that I know nothing.'
DJ Khaled: 'You know!'

example_sentence: Please write your name here.

example_translation.es: Por favor escriba su nombre aquí.
example_translation.de: Bitte schreiben Sie hier Ihren Namen.
example_translation.fr: Veuillez écrire votre nom ici.
example_translation.pt: Por favor, escreva seu nome aqui.
example_translation.it: Per favore scrivi il tuo nome qui.
example_translation.ja: ここにお名前を書いてください。
example_translation.zh: 请在这里写上你的名字。

culturalContext: Writing is a cornerstone of English-speaking education and culture. From Shakespeare to social media posts, written English shapes communication.
usageNotes: Irregular: write-wrote-written. 'Write down' = note. 'Write up' = formal version. 'Write off' = dismiss or financial loss. 'Writer's block' = inability to write.
funFact: English is written in the Latin alphabet, but only about 40% of English words are spelled the way they sound, making spelling notoriously difficult.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: write-wrote-written. Transitive and intransitive. 'Write to someone' (letter), 'write about something.'
commonMistakes: Past forms: 'writed' (wrong — 'wrote/written')
Confusing 'write,' 'right,' and 'rite' — homophones
realWorldExamples: Shakespeare: the most famous English writer
Stephen King: 'On Writing' — writing advice book
Taylor Swift: famous for writing her own songs

example_sentence: I like to read before going to sleep.

example_translation.es: Me gusta leer antes de dormir.
example_translation.de: Ich lese gerne vor dem Einschlafen.
example_translation.fr: J'aime lire avant de m'endormir.
example_translation.pt: Gosto de ler antes de dormir.
example_translation.it: Mi piace leggere prima di dormire.
example_translation.ja: 寝る前に読書するのが好きです。
example_translation.ko: 자기 전에 책 읽는 것을 좋아해요.
example_translation.zh: 我喜欢睡前阅读。

culturalContext: Reading culture is promoted in English-speaking countries through libraries, book clubs, and literacy programs. 'Reading for pleasure' is considered essential for education.
usageNotes: Irregular: read-read-read (pronunciation changes: /riːd/-/rɛd/-/rɛd/). 'Read' also = interpret: 'read someone's mind,' 'read the room.'
funFact: The past tense of 'read' is spelled the same but pronounced differently (/rɛd/ like 'red'), making it one of English's trickiest verbs.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: read /riːd/ - read /rɛd/ - read /rɛd/. Same spelling, different pronunciation. 'Read about/on' (topic).
sentencePatterns: She reads the news every morning.
commonMistakes: Pronunciation: past tense 'read' sounds like 'red'
'Read' the room = understand the social situation (figurative)
realWorldExamples: Dr. Seuss: 'The more that you read...'
LeVar Burton: Reading Rainbow
Rihanna: Reading Is Fundamental — charity

example_sentence: She speaks three languages fluently.

example_translation.es: Ella habla tres idiomas con fluidez.
example_translation.de: Sie spricht drei Sprachen fließend.
example_translation.fr: Elle parle couramment trois langues.
example_translation.pt: Ela fala três idiomas fluentemente.
example_translation.it: Parla tre lingue correntemente.
example_translation.ru: Она свободно говорит на трёх языках.
example_translation.ja: 彼女は3か国語を流暢に話します。
example_translation.ko: 그녀는 세 개 국어를 유창하게 해요.
example_translation.zh: 她能流利地说三种语言。

culturalContext: Speaking ability is highly valued in English-speaking professional culture. Public speaking, TED talks, and eloquence are culturally important skills.
usageNotes: Irregular: speak-spoke-spoken. 'Speak' vs 'talk': 'speak' is more formal. 'Speak up' = louder or express opinion. 'So to speak' = figuratively.
funFact: The fear of public speaking (glossophobia) affects up to 75% of English speakers, making it more feared than death in many surveys.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: speak-spoke-spoken. 'Speak to/with' someone. 'Speak' is more formal than 'talk.' 'Speaker' = noun.
commonMistakes: Past: 'speaked' (wrong — 'spoke')
'Speak to' vs 'speak with' — 'to' can imply one-way, 'with' implies conversation
realWorldExamples: Martin Luther King Jr.: 'I Have a Dream' speech
TED Talks: 'Ideas worth spreading'
Phone: 'May I speak to [name]?'

example_sentence: Listen carefully to the instructions.

example_translation.es: Escucha atentamente las instrucciones.
example_translation.de: Höre aufmerksam den Anweisungen zu.
example_translation.fr: Écoute attentivement les instructions.
example_translation.pt: Ouça atentamente as instruções.
example_translation.it: Ascolta attentamente le istruzioni.
example_translation.ja: 指示をよく聞いてください。
example_translation.zh: 请仔细听指示。

culturalContext: Active listening is a valued skill in English-speaking education and workplace culture. 'Listen' implies intentional attention, unlike 'hear.'
usageNotes: 'Listen to' + noun (always with 'to'). 'Listen' = intentional. 'Hear' = perceive sound (possibly unintentional). 'Listen up!' = pay attention (imperative).
funFact: Studies show that people remember only 25-50% of what they hear, which is why 'Are you even listening?' is such a common English complaint.
grammarNote: Regular verb: listen-listened-listened. Always 'listen to' (never 'listen' + direct object). Intransitive verb.
commonMistakes: Omitting 'to': 'listen music' (wrong — 'listen to music')
Confusing 'listen' (intentional) with 'hear' (perception)
realWorldExamples: Beyonce: 'Listen' from Dreamgirls
Simon & Garfunkel: 'The Sound of Silence' — people not listening
Common parenting: 'Listen to me!'

example_sentence: Can I ask you a question?

example_translation.es: ¿Puedo hacerte una pregunta?
example_translation.de: Kann ich dir eine Frage stellen?
example_translation.fr: Puis-je te poser une question ?
example_translation.pt: Posso fazer uma pergunta?
example_translation.it: Posso farti una domanda?
example_translation.ja: 質問してもいいですか？
example_translation.zh: 我可以问你一个问题吗？

culturalContext: Asking questions is encouraged in English-speaking education ('there are no stupid questions'). However, asking the wrong questions in social settings can be considered rude.
usageNotes: 'Ask' + person + question. 'Ask for' = request. 'Ask about' = inquire. 'Ask out' = invite on a date. 'If you ask me' = in my opinion.
funFact: Children ask an average of 300 questions per day, but this drops dramatically by adulthood — English education tries to encourage lifelong questioning.
grammarNote: Regular verb. 'Ask someone something' (double object). 'Ask for' (request). 'Ask about' (inquire). No preposition before person.
sentencePatterns: Can I ask you a question?
commonMistakes: Word order: 'ask to him' (wrong — 'ask him')
Confusing 'ask' and 'ask for': 'ask the price' vs 'ask for help'
realWorldExamples: Classroom: 'Any questions? Don't be afraid to ask.'
Common phrase: 'Don't ask me!'
Billboard: 'Ask your doctor about...'

example_sentence: Please answer my question.

example_translation.es: Por favor responde mi pregunta.
example_translation.de: Bitte beantworte meine Frage.
example_translation.fr: Réponds à ma question, s'il te plaît.
example_translation.pt: Por favor, responda minha pergunta.
example_translation.it: Per favore rispondi alla mia domanda.
example_translation.ja: 質問に答えてください。
example_translation.zh: 请回答我的问题。

culturalContext: Answering and response culture is important in English communication. 'The answer to life, the universe, and everything' (42 — Douglas Adams) is a beloved cultural reference.
usageNotes: 'Answer' + question/phone/door (no preposition needed for direct objects). 'The answer to' a question. Noun and verb. 'Answer back' = respond rudely.
funFact: In Douglas Adams' 'Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy,' the answer to life, the universe, and everything is 42 — one of the most famous answers in English literature.
grammarNote: Transitive verb and countable noun. 'Answer the question/phone/door' (no preposition). 'Answer to' as noun: 'the answer to the problem.'
commonMistakes: Adding preposition: 'answer to the question' (verb — 'answer the question')
Confusing 'answer' with 'reply': 'answer' is broader (phone, door, questions)
realWorldExamples: Hitchhiker's Guide: 'The answer is 42.'
Who Wants to Be a Millionaire: 'Is that your final answer?'
Iverson: 'We're talking about practice, not a game. Not a game. Not a game.'

example_sentence: This restaurant is too expensive.

example_translation.es: Este restaurante es demasiado caro.
example_translation.de: Dieses Restaurant ist zu teuer.
example_translation.fr: Ce restaurant est trop cher.
example_translation.pt: Este restaurante é muito caro.
example_translation.it: Questo ristorante è troppo costoso.
example_translation.ja: このレストランは高すぎます。
example_translation.zh: 这家餐厅太贵了。

culturalContext: Cost of living discussions dominate English-speaking media. 'Expensive' is relative — what's expensive in one English-speaking country may be normal in another.
usageNotes: 'Expensive' for high cost. Gradations: pricey < expensive < overpriced < exorbitant. 'Expensive taste' = preference for luxury.
funFact: Switzerland and Norway consistently rank as the most expensive countries in the world, while India and Vietnam are among the least expensive.
grammarNote: Adjective. Comparative: more expensive. Superlative: most expensive. Related: expense (noun), expensively (adverb).
commonMistakes: Using 'expensiver' (wrong — 'more expensive')
Confusing 'expensive' (adj, for things) with 'costly' (can also describe consequences)
realWorldExamples: Real estate: 'Property in London is extremely expensive.'
Bruno Mars: 'I wanna buy you expensive things.'
Common complaint: 'Everything is so expensive these days!'

example_sentence: I found a cheap flight to London.

example_translation.es: Encontré un vuelo barato a Londres.
example_translation.de: Ich habe einen billigen Flug nach London gefunden.
example_translation.fr: J'ai trouvé un vol pas cher pour Londres.
example_translation.pt: Encontrei um voo barato para Londres.
example_translation.it: Ho trovato un volo economico per Londra.
example_translation.ru: Я нашёл дешёвый рейс в Лондон.
example_translation.ja: ロンドン行きの安い航空券を見つけました。
example_translation.zh: 我找到了一张去伦敦的便宜机票。

culturalContext: 'Cheap' carries both positive (affordable) and negative (low quality, stingy) connotations in English. Being called 'cheap' as a person is an insult.
usageNotes: 'Cheap' can be negative (low quality) or positive (affordable). 'Cheap' about a person = stingy (insult). Better alternatives: 'affordable,' 'inexpensive,' 'budget-friendly.'
funFact: The phrase 'cheap shot' (unfair attack) comes from 1960s American sports slang and is now used broadly for any unfair criticism.
grammarNote: Adjective. Comparative: cheaper. Superlative: cheapest. Can be adverb: 'buy cheap.' 'Cheaply' = adverb (more formal).
commonMistakes: Using 'cheap' for people (insulting — means stingy)
Not knowing 'inexpensive' is the polite alternative to 'cheap'
realWorldExamples: IKEA: affordable furniture empire
Sia: 'Cheap Thrills'
Common: 'You get what you pay for' — implying cheap = low quality

example_sentence: What a beautiful sunset!

example_translation.es: ¡Qué hermoso atardecer!
example_translation.de: Was für ein schöner Sonnenuntergang!
example_translation.fr: Quel beau coucher de soleil !
example_translation.pt: Que pôr do sol bonito!
example_translation.it: Che bel tramonto!
example_translation.ja: なんて美しい夕焼けでしょう！
example_translation.zh: 多美的日落啊！

culturalContext: Beauty standards are a major cultural discussion in English-speaking media. 'Beautiful' is one of the most powerful compliments in English.
usageNotes: 'Beautiful' for aesthetics and deeper appreciation. Stronger than 'pretty' or 'nice-looking.' Can describe non-physical things: 'a beautiful mind,' 'a beautiful day.'
funFact: The most-searched beauty-related English word online is 'beautiful,' surpassing 'pretty,' 'gorgeous,' and 'stunning' combined.
grammarNote: Adjective. 'Beautiful' is ungradable in theory but commonly intensified: 'absolutely beautiful.' 'Beautifully' = adverb.
commonMistakes: Spelling: 'beautifull' (wrong — one 'l')
Using 'beautiful' for men (acceptable but 'handsome' is more traditional)
realWorldExamples: Christina Aguilera: 'Beautiful'
A Beautiful Mind (2001) — Russell Crowe
James Blunt: 'You're Beautiful'

example_sentence: This exercise is very easy.

example_translation.es: Este ejercicio es muy fácil.
example_translation.de: Diese Übung ist sehr einfach.
example_translation.fr: Cet exercice est très facile.
example_translation.pt: Este exercício é muito fácil.
example_translation.it: Questo esercizio è molto facile.
example_translation.ja: この練習はとても簡単です。
example_translation.zh: 这个练习很容易。

culturalContext: 'Easy' connects to the English-speaking value of simplicity and accessibility. 'Easy-going,' 'take it easy,' and 'easy does it' reflect a laid-back cultural ideal.
usageNotes: 'Easy' as adjective or adverb (informal: 'take it easy'). 'Easy-going' = relaxed personality. 'Easier said than done' = common phrase. 'Easy on the eyes' = attractive.
funFact: The Staples 'Easy Button' became one of the most successful advertising gimmicks in American history, selling millions of novelty buttons.
grammarNote: Adjective. Comparative: easier. Superlative: easiest. 'Easily' = adverb. 'Easy' as informal adverb: 'Go easy on him.'
commonMistakes: Using 'easy' as adverb in formal writing (use 'easily')
Confusing 'easy' with 'simple' (easy = not difficult, simple = not complex)
realWorldExamples: The Eagles: 'Take It Easy'
Staples: 'That was easy!'
Lionel Richie: 'Easy Like Sunday Morning'

example_sentence: The exam was very difficult.

example_translation.es: El examen fue muy difícil.
example_translation.de: Die Prüfung war sehr schwierig.
example_translation.fr: L'examen était très difficile.
example_translation.pt: A prova foi muito difícil.
example_translation.it: L'esame era molto difficile.
example_translation.ja: 試験はとても難しかったです。
example_translation.zh: 考试非常难。

culturalContext: Difficulty and challenge are viewed positively in English-speaking cultures: 'No pain, no gain,' 'what doesn't kill you makes you stronger' — struggle is valued.
usageNotes: 'Difficult' is neutral/formal. 'Hard' is more casual. 'Tough' implies requiring endurance. 'Difficult' + to-infinitive or + for + person.
funFact: The phrase 'when the going gets tough, the tough get going' was popularized by Joseph Kennedy and later became a Billy Ocean hit song.
grammarNote: Adjective. 'Difficult to do' or 'difficult for someone to do.' 'Difficulty' = noun (with difficulty). More formal than 'hard.'
commonMistakes: 'Difficult' vs 'hard': interchangeable but 'difficult' is more formal
'Have difficulty' + gerund (not infinitive): 'difficulty understanding' not 'difficulty to understand'
realWorldExamples: Billy Ocean: 'When the Going Gets Tough'
Tom Hanks: 'There's no crying in baseball!' — difficulty accepted
Common interview question: 'Tell me about a difficult situation you handled.'

example_sentence: He is a very fast runner.

example_translation.es: Es un corredor muy rápido.
example_translation.de: Er ist ein sehr schneller Läufer.
example_translation.fr: C'est un coureur très rapide.
example_translation.pt: Ele é um corredor muito rápido.
example_translation.it: È un corridore molto veloce.
example_translation.ja: 彼はとても速いランナーです。
example_translation.zh: 他是一个非常快的跑步者。

culturalContext: Speed is valued in English-speaking cultures: 'fast food,' 'fast-track,' 'fast lane.' The emphasis on efficiency and speed is particularly American.
usageNotes: 'Fast' as adjective and adverb (no '-ly' needed). 'Fast food,' 'fast track,' 'fast forward.' 'Fast' also = not eating (religious/health context).
funFact: 'Fast food' was coined in the 1950s in America and has become a global English loanword used in virtually every language.
grammarNote: Adjective and adverb (same form). No need for 'fastly' (doesn't exist). Also noun/verb for not eating: 'to fast,' 'a fast.'
commonMistakes: Using 'fastly' (doesn't exist — 'fast' is already an adverb)
Not knowing 'fast' also means 'not eating'
realWorldExamples: Fast & Furious franchise
McDonald's: fast food empire
Intermittent fasting: 'I'm fasting today.'

example_sentence: Please speak more slowly.

example_translation.es: Por favor habla más lento.
example_translation.de: Bitte sprich langsamer.
example_translation.fr: Parle plus lentement, s'il te plaît.
example_translation.pt: Por favor, fale mais devagar.
example_translation.it: Per favore parla più lentamente.
example_translation.ja: もっとゆっくり話してください。
example_translation.zh: 请说慢一点。

culturalContext: 'Slow' has been reclaimed positively: 'slow food,' 'slow living,' 'slow fashion' — countering the fast-paced English-speaking lifestyle.
usageNotes: 'Slow' adjective and adverb ('go slow'). 'Slowly' is the formal adverb. 'Slow down' = reduce speed. 'Slow motion' = replay technique.
funFact: The 'Slow Food' movement, founded in Italy in 1986, now has English-speaking chapters worldwide as a counter to fast food culture.
grammarNote: Adjective and informal adverb ('drive slow'). 'Slowly' = standard adverb. 'Slow down' = phrasal verb. 'Slow motion' = compound noun.
commonMistakes: 'Slow' vs 'slowly' as adverb — 'slow' is informal, 'slowly' is standard
Confusing 'slow' with 'low' in some accents
realWorldExamples: Slow Food movement: countering fast food
Beyonce: 'Slow down' — song theme
Internet complaint: 'Why is the Wi-Fi so slow?'

example_sentence: The class begins at nine o'clock.

example_translation.es: La clase empieza a las nueve.
example_translation.de: Der Unterricht beginnt um neun Uhr.
example_translation.fr: Le cours commence à neuf heures.
example_translation.pt: A aula começa às nove horas.
example_translation.it: La lezione inizia alle nove.
example_translation.ja: 授業は9時に始まります。
example_translation.zh: 课程九点开始。

culturalContext: Beginnings carry optimism in English culture: 'new beginnings,' 'a fresh start,' 'from the beginning.' Every January brings 'begin again' energy.
usageNotes: Irregular: begin-began-begun. More formal than 'start.' 'Begin with' = start by. 'Beginner' = novice. 'Beginning' = start (noun).
funFact: The phrase 'In the beginning' opens both the Bible and Tolkien's 'The Silmarillion,' making it one of the most iconic opening lines in English.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: begin-began-begun. 'Begin' + gerund or infinitive. More formal than 'start.' 'Beginning' = noun.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'beginned' (wrong — 'began')
Confusing 'begin' and 'start' — 'begin' is more formal but often interchangeable
realWorldExamples: Bible: 'In the beginning, God created...'
Black Eyed Peas: 'Let's Get It Started'
Common: 'Let's begin, shall we?'

example_sentence: I need to finish this report today.

example_translation.es: Necesito terminar este informe hoy.
example_translation.de: Ich muss diesen Bericht heute beenden.
example_translation.fr: Je dois finir ce rapport aujourd'hui.
example_translation.pt: Preciso terminar este relatório hoje.
example_translation.it: Devo finire questo rapporto oggi.
example_translation.ru: Мне нужно закончить этот отчёт сегодня.
example_translation.ja: 今日このレポートを終えなければなりません。
example_translation.zh: 我今天需要完成这份报告。

culturalContext: Finishing and completion are celebrated in English culture: 'finish line,' 'finishing touch,' graduation ceremonies. 'Finisher' = someone who completes what they start.
usageNotes: 'Finish' + gerund: 'finish eating.' 'Finish off/up' = complete entirely. 'Finish line' = end of race. 'Finished' = done or ruined.
funFact: Marathon runners who cross the finish line get 'finisher medals' — the concept of finishing as achievement is deeply English.
grammarNote: Regular verb. 'Finish' + gerund (not infinitive): 'finish eating' (not 'finish to eat'). 'Finished' = adjective meaning done.
commonMistakes: 'Finish to do' (wrong — 'finish doing')
Confusing 'finish' with 'end': finish = complete a task, end = come to a close
realWorldExamples: Mortal Kombat: 'Finish him!'
Marathon culture: crossing the finish line
Common: 'Are you finished?' (done eating/working)

example_sentence: I live in a small apartment.

example_translation.es: Vivo en un pequeño apartamento.
example_translation.de: Ich lebe in einer kleinen Wohnung.
example_translation.fr: Je vis dans un petit appartement.
example_translation.pt: Moro em um apartamento pequeno.
example_translation.it: Vivo in un piccolo appartamento.
example_translation.ja: 小さなアパートに住んでいます。
example_translation.zh: 我住在一间小公寓里。

culturalContext: Living and lifestyle are central English concepts. 'Live your best life,' 'live and let live,' and 'live in the moment' reflect cultural values.
usageNotes: Two pronunciations: /lɪv/ (verb: to live) and /laɪv/ (adjective: live music). 'Live' vs 'alive' — 'alive' is predicative only ('He is alive').
funFact: 'Live' as in 'live performance' comes from the early days of radio/TV when 'live' meant unrecorded, as opposed to pre-recorded.
grammarNote: Verb /lɪv/: live-lived-lived. Adjective /laɪv/: live music, live broadcast. 'Alive' = predicative adjective.
commonMistakes: Pronunciation: 'live' verb (/lɪv/) vs 'live' adjective (/laɪv/)
'Life' (noun) vs 'live' (verb) vs 'alive' (adjective)
realWorldExamples: Bon Jovi: 'It's My Life'
SNL: 'Live from New York, it's Saturday Night!'
Drake: 'YOLO — You Only Live Once'

example_sentence: I walk to the park every morning.

example_translation.es: Camino al parque cada mañana.
example_translation.de: Ich gehe jeden Morgen zum Park.
example_translation.fr: Je marche jusqu'au parc chaque matin.
example_translation.pt: Eu caminho até o parque toda manhã.
example_translation.it: Cammino fino al parco ogni mattina.
example_translation.ru: Каждое утро я хожу в парк.
example_translation.ja: 毎朝公園まで歩きます。
example_translation.zh: 我每天早上走路去公园。

culturalContext: Walking culture varies: London is walkable, while most American cities are car-dependent. 'Walk' extends to figurative use: 'walk the walk,' 'walk of life.'
usageNotes: 'Walk' + adverb/preposition for direction. 'Go for a walk' = take a walk. 'Walk away' = leave. 'Walk of life' = social background. 'Walk the talk' = match actions to words.
funFact: The average Londoner walks approximately 900 miles per year, while the average Los Angeles resident walks only about 350 miles.
grammarNote: Regular verb. Also a noun: 'go for a walk.' 'Walk' as informal noun: 'a 10-minute walk.' Many phrasal verbs: walk out, walk in, walk away.
commonMistakes: 'Go to walk' (wrong — 'go for a walk')
Confusing 'walk' with 'work' in pronunciation (some accents)
realWorldExamples: Johnny Cash: 'I Walk the Line'
The Proclaimers: 'I would walk 500 miles'
Walk of Fame: Hollywood Boulevard

example_sentence: I run five kilometers every morning.

example_translation.es: Corro cinco kilómetros cada mañana.
example_translation.de: Ich laufe jeden Morgen fünf Kilometer.
example_translation.fr: Je cours cinq kilomètres chaque matin.
example_translation.pt: Eu corro cinco quilômetros toda manhã.
example_translation.it: Corro cinque chilometri ogni mattina.
example_translation.ru: Каждое утро я бегаю пять километров.
example_translation.ja: 毎朝5キロ走っています。
example_translation.zh: 我每天早上跑五公里。

culturalContext: Running culture is huge in English-speaking countries: marathons, parkrun, Couch to 5K. 'Run' also dominates business: 'run a company,' 'in the long run.'
usageNotes: Irregular: run-ran-run. Extremely versatile: 'run a business,' 'run out of,' 'run into' (meet), 'run late,' 'run for office.' Physical and figurative.
funFact: Parkrun, a free weekly 5K run that started in London in 2004, now operates in 22 countries with millions of regular runners.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: run-ran-run. One of the most versatile verbs in English with dozens of phrasal verbs and figurative meanings.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'runned' (wrong — 'ran')
Not knowing the many figurative meanings: run out, run into, run for
realWorldExamples: Forrest Gump: 'Run, Forrest, run!'
Parkrun: global running movement
Business: 'Who runs this company?'

example_sentence: The children play in the garden after school.

example_translation.es: Los niños juegan en el jardín después de la escuela.
example_translation.de: Die Kinder spielen nach der Schule im Garten.
example_translation.fr: Les enfants jouent dans le jardin après l'école.
example_translation.pt: As crianças brincam no jardim depois da escola.
example_translation.it: I bambini giocano in giardino dopo la scuola.
example_translation.ru: Дети играют в саду после школы.
example_translation.ja: 子供たちは放課後に庭で遊びます。
example_translation.zh: 孩子们放学后在花园里玩。

culturalContext: Play is valued for children and adults in English culture. 'Play' extends to music, theater, and games. 'Fair play' is a cherished British value.
usageNotes: 'Play' + sport (no article): 'play tennis.' 'Play' + instrument (with 'the'): 'play the piano.' 'Play' = drama (noun). 'Fair play' = justice/sportsmanship.
funFact: Shakespeare wrote 37 plays — the word 'play' for theatrical performance comes from Old English 'plega' meaning exercise or activity.
grammarNote: Regular verb. 'Play' + sport (no article). 'Play' + the + instrument. Also countable noun (theatrical). 'Player' = participant.
commonMistakes: Article usage: 'play football' (no article) vs 'play the piano' (article needed for instruments)
'Play' a role vs 'play' a sport — different preposition patterns
realWorldExamples: Shakespeare's plays: 'All the world's a stage.'
Google: 'Google Play' Store
Common: 'Fair play!' (BrE — acknowledging good sportsmanship)

example_sentence: My mother likes to cook Italian food.

example_translation.es: A mi madre le gusta cocinar comida italiana.
example_translation.de: Meine Mutter kocht gerne italienisch.
example_translation.fr: Ma mère aime cuisiner des plats italiens.
example_translation.pt: Minha mãe gosta de cozinhar comida italiana.
example_translation.it: A mia madre piace cucinare cibo italiano.
example_translation.ru: Моя мама любит готовить итальянскую еду.
example_translation.ja: 母はイタリア料理を作るのが好きです。
example_translation.zh: 我妈妈喜欢做意大利菜。

culturalContext: Cooking culture has exploded in English-speaking countries via shows like MasterChef, Bake Off, and celebrity chefs. 'Cook' is both skill and identity.
usageNotes: 'Cook' as verb and noun (person who cooks). 'Chef' = professional cook. 'Cook up' = invent/improvise. 'What's cooking?' = what's happening?
funFact: The Great British Bake Off (2010-present) revived home baking culture in the UK and became a global phenomenon.
grammarNote: Regular verb and countable noun. 'Cook' (home) vs 'chef' (professional). 'Cooking' as noun/gerund: 'I love cooking.'
commonMistakes: Confusing 'cook' with 'chef' — a cook is anyone, a chef is a trained professional
'Cook' vs 'cooker' — 'cooker' in BrE is the appliance, not the person
realWorldExamples: Ratatouille: 'Anyone can cook.'
Gordon Ramsay: MasterChef
The Great British Bake Off

example_sentence: The weather is nice today.

example_translation.es: El clima está agradable hoy.
example_translation.de: Das Wetter ist heute schön.
example_translation.fr: Il fait beau aujourd'hui.
example_translation.pt: O tempo está bom hoje.
example_translation.it: Il tempo è bello oggi.
example_translation.ja: 今日はいい天気です。
example_translation.zh: 今天天气很好。

culturalContext: Weather is the quintessential English small-talk topic, especially in the UK. The British obsession with weather reflects the country's unpredictable climate.
usageNotes: Uncountable: 'the weather.' 'Weather' as verb: 'weather a storm' (survive difficulty). 'Weather forecast,' 'bad/good weather,' 'under the weather' = feeling sick.
funFact: The British Met Office issues around 1,500 weather warnings per year, feeding the UK's national obsession with weather discussion.
grammarNote: Uncountable noun (always 'the weather'). Also a verb: 'weather a storm.' 'Under the weather' = feeling ill.
commonMistakes: 'How is the weather?' vs 'What is the weather like?' — both correct but the latter is more standard
Confusing 'weather' with 'whether' (conjunction) or 'wether' (castrated sheep)
realWorldExamples: British small talk: 'Lovely weather, isn't it?'
Climate change discussions dominate weather coverage
Paul Simon: 'The only living boy in New York' — weather imagery

example_sentence: The children love playing in the snow.

example_translation.es: A los niños les encanta jugar en la nieve.
example_translation.de: Die Kinder spielen gerne im Schnee.
example_translation.fr: Les enfants adorent jouer dans la neige.
example_translation.pt: As crianças adoram brincar na neve.
example_translation.it: I bambini adorano giocare nella neve.
example_translation.ja: 子供たちは雪の中で遊ぶのが大好きです。
example_translation.zh: 孩子们喜欢在雪地里玩。

culturalContext: Snow carries magical associations in English culture: 'White Christmas,' snow days off school, and winter wonderland imagery.
usageNotes: Uncountable: 'snow' (substance). 'A snowfall/snowstorm.' 'Snowy' = adjective. 'Snow day' = school closed due to snow (AmE). 'Snowflake' = delicate person (modern slang).
funFact: The Inuit languages are famous for having many words for snow, but English also has dozens: slush, sleet, flurry, blizzard, powder, drift, etc.
grammarNote: Uncountable noun. Also impersonal verb: 'It's snowing.' Related: snowfall, snowstorm, snowflake, snowy.
sentencePatterns: We had a lot of snow this winter.
commonMistakes: Pluralizing: 'snows' only valid for poetic/literary use
Impersonal verb: 'Is snowing' (wrong — 'It is snowing')
realWorldExamples: Bing Crosby: 'White Christmas' — best-selling single ever
Game of Thrones: 'Winter is coming' + Jon Snow
Disney's Frozen: 'Do You Want to Build a Snowman?'

example_sentence: We grow vegetables in our garden.

example_translation.es: Cultivamos verduras en nuestro jardín.
example_translation.de: Wir bauen Gemüse in unserem Garten an.
example_translation.fr: Nous cultivons des légumes dans notre jardin.
example_translation.pt: Cultivamos legumes em nosso jardim.
example_translation.it: Coltiviamo verdure nel nostro giardino.
example_translation.ru: Мы выращиваем овощи в нашем саду.
example_translation.ja: 私たちの庭で野菜を育てています。
example_translation.zh: 我们在花园里种蔬菜。

culturalContext: Gardens are beloved in English culture, especially British. 'The English garden' is a recognized landscape style. Gardening is one of Britain's most popular hobbies.
usageNotes: 'Garden' in BrE = backyard (AmE). 'Garden' as verb: 'I love gardening.' 'Garden party' = formal outdoor event. 'Garden-variety' = ordinary.
funFact: The Chelsea Flower Show, held annually in London since 1913, is the world's most prestigious garden show and a highlight of the British social calendar.
grammarNote: Countable noun. Also a verb: 'to garden.' BrE 'garden' often = AmE 'yard/backyard.' 'Gardener' = person. 'Gardening' = activity.
commonMistakes: BrE 'garden' vs AmE 'yard' — different default meanings
Confusing 'garden' with 'park' (garden = private, park = public)
realWorldExamples: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett
Chelsea Flower Show — quintessentially British
Octopus's Garden — The Beatles

example_sentence: It takes eight hours to fly to London.

example_translation.es: Se tarda ocho horas en volar a Londres.
example_translation.de: Es dauert acht Stunden, um nach London zu fliegen.
example_translation.fr: Il faut huit heures pour voler jusqu'à Londres.
example_translation.pt: Leva oito horas para voar até Londres.
example_translation.it: Ci vogliono otto ore per volare a Londra.
example_translation.ja: ロンドンまで飛行機で8時間かかります。
example_translation.zh: 飞到伦敦需要八个小时。

culturalContext: Flying represents freedom and aspiration in English culture: 'fly high,' 'spread your wings,' 'the sky's the limit.' Air travel democratized global movement.
usageNotes: Irregular: fly-flew-flown. 'Fly' = travel by plane, move through air, go quickly. 'Fly-by-night' = unreliable. 'Fly off the handle' = lose temper.
funFact: The Wright Brothers' first flight in 1903 lasted just 12 seconds — now over 100,000 flights operate daily worldwide.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: fly-flew-flown. Also a noun (insect). 'Fly' as adjective (slang): cool/stylish. 'Flies' = plural noun.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'flied' (wrong for most meanings — 'flew'; 'flied' only in baseball: 'flied out')
Confusing 'fly' (verb) with 'fly' (insect)
realWorldExamples: Frank Sinatra: 'Fly Me to the Moon'
R. Kelly: 'I Believe I Can Fly'
Peter Pan: 'All you need is faith, trust, and a little bit of pixie dust to fly.'

example_sentence: I will send you an email tomorrow.

example_translation.es: Te enviaré un correo electrónico mañana.
example_translation.de: Ich werde dir morgen eine E-Mail senden.
example_translation.fr: Je t'enverrai un e-mail demain.
example_translation.pt: Vou te enviar um e-mail amanhã.
example_translation.it: Ti invierò un'e-mail domani.
example_translation.ja: 明日メールを送ります。
example_translation.zh: 我明天给你发邮件。

culturalContext: Sending messages has transformed with technology — from letters to emails to instant messaging. 'Send' captures modern communication culture.
usageNotes: Irregular: send-sent-sent. 'Send' + indirect object + direct object: 'Send me a message.' 'Send for' = summon. 'Send off' = dispatch or farewell.
funFact: The first email was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson to himself — he later said the content was 'something like QWERTYUIOP.'
grammarNote: Irregular verb: send-sent-sent. Double object: 'send someone something.' 'Send for' = summon. 'Send off' = mail or farewell.
commonMistakes: Past tense: 'sended' (wrong — 'sent')
Word order: 'send to me it' (wrong — 'send it to me' or 'send me it')
realWorldExamples: Adele: 'Send My Love (To Your New Lover)'
iPhone: 'Send' button
Email culture: 'I'll send you the details.'

example_sentence: Did you receive my message?

example_translation.es: ¿Recibiste mi mensaje?
example_translation.de: Hast du meine Nachricht empfangen?
example_translation.fr: As-tu reçu mon message ?
example_translation.pt: Você recebeu minha mensagem?
example_translation.it: Hai ricevuto il mio messaggio?
example_translation.ja: 私のメッセージは届きましたか？
example_translation.zh: 你收到我的消息了吗？

culturalContext: Receiving — gifts, news, feedback — is culturally shaped in English. 'It's better to give than to receive' reflects English-speaking charitable values.
usageNotes: 'Receive' is formal; 'get' is the everyday equivalent. 'Receive' a letter/award/guest. 'On the receiving end' = being affected by something.
funFact: English has two distinct verbs ('give' and 'receive') while some languages use a single verb with directional markers.
grammarNote: Regular verb. More formal than 'get.' 'Receive' + noun. 'Receiver' = person receiving or phone handset. 'Receipt' = proof of purchase.
commonMistakes: Spelling: 'recieve' (wrong — 'receive'; remember 'i before e except after c')
Using 'receive' in casual speech (too formal — use 'get')
realWorldExamples: Award ceremonies: 'I'm honored to receive this award.'
Email: 'We received your application.'
Proverb: 'It's better to give than to receive.'

example_sentence: You should wear a warm coat today.

example_translation.es: Deberías llevar un abrigo cálido hoy.
example_translation.de: Du solltest heute einen warmen Mantel tragen.
example_translation.fr: Tu devrais porter un manteau chaud aujourd'hui.
example_translation.pt: Você deveria vestir um casaco quente hoje.
example_translation.it: Dovresti indossare un cappotto caldo oggi.
example_translation.ru: Тебе стоит надеть тёплое пальто сегодня.
example_translation.ja: 今日は暖かいコートを着た方がいいですよ。
example_translation.zh: 你今天应该穿一件暖和的外套。

culturalContext: Fashion and clothing are significant in English-speaking pop culture. 'What are you wearing?' is common conversation. 'Wear and tear' = everyday damage.
usageNotes: Irregular: wear-wore-worn. 'Wear' for clothing, accessories, hairstyles. 'Wear out' = exhaust or become unusable. 'Wear off' = gradually disappear.
funFact: The fashion industry is worth over $2.5 trillion globally, and English is its primary language of commerce and media.
grammarNote: Irregular verb: wear-wore-worn. 'Wear' for clothes, accessories, expressions. 'Wear' as noun: 'wear and tear.' Phrasal verbs: wear out, wear off.
commonMistakes: Past: 'weared' (wrong — 'wore')
Confusing 'wear' with 'put on': 'wear' = have on body, 'put on' = the act of dressing
realWorldExamples: The Devil Wears Prada (2006)
Common question: 'What are you going to wear?'
Red carpet: 'Who are you wearing?' (which designer)

example_sentence: I need a glass of water.

example_translation.es: Necesito un vaso de agua.
example_translation.de: Ich brauche ein Glas Wasser.
example_translation.fr: J'ai besoin d'un verre d'eau.
example_translation.pt: Preciso de um copo de água.
example_translation.it: Ho bisogno di un bicchiere d'acqua.
example_translation.ja: 水を一杯ください。
example_translation.zh: 我需要一杯水。

culturalContext: Needs vs wants is a fundamental distinction in English-speaking economics and self-help culture. Maslow's hierarchy of needs is widely referenced.
usageNotes: 'Need' as verb: 'need to do' or 'need doing' (BrE passive meaning). As noun: 'a need for.' 'In need' = requiring help. 'No need' = unnecessary.
funFact: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs (1943), taught in virtually every English-speaking psychology class, has become a universal cultural reference.
grammarNote: Modal-like verb and regular verb. 'Need to do' (obligation). 'Need doing' (BrE: passive meaning, 'needs to be done'). Also a noun.
commonMistakes: BrE 'needs doing' = AmE 'needs to be done'
Confusing 'need' (necessity) with 'want' (desire)
realWorldExamples: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs — psychology classic
Cheap Trick: 'I Want You to Want Me' — need vs want
Common: 'I need a vacation!'

example_sentence: I want to travel the world.

example_translation.es: Quiero viajar por el mundo.
example_translation.de: Ich möchte die Welt bereisen.
example_translation.fr: Je veux voyager à travers le monde.
example_translation.pt: Quero viajar pelo mundo.
example_translation.it: Voglio viaggiare per il mondo.
example_translation.ja: 世界を旅したいです。
example_translation.zh: 我想环游世界。

culturalContext: Wanting and desire drive English-speaking consumer culture. 'I want it all' and 'you can't always get what you want' represent cultural tension around desire.
usageNotes: 'Want' + noun or + to-infinitive. More direct than 'would like' (polite). 'Want' can sound demanding: 'I want a coffee' vs 'I'd like a coffee, please.'
funFact: The Rolling Stones' 'You Can't Always Get What You Want' was ranked #100 on Rolling Stone's list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.
grammarNote: Regular verb. 'Want to' (often contracted to 'wanna' in speech). 'Want' + object + infinitive: 'I want you to come.'
sentencePatterns: I don't want to be rude.
commonMistakes: 'Want' is more direct/less polite than 'would like'
Informal 'wanna' should not be used in formal writing
realWorldExamples: Spice Girls: 'Tell me what you want, what you really really want.'
Rolling Stones: 'You Can't Always Get What You Want'
Queen: 'I Want It All'

example_sentence: You should try this new restaurant.

example_translation.es: Deberías probar este nuevo restaurante.
example_translation.de: Du solltest dieses neue Restaurant ausprobieren.
example_translation.fr: Tu devrais essayer ce nouveau restaurant.
example_translation.pt: Você deveria experimentar este novo restaurante.
example_translation.it: Dovresti provare questo nuovo ristorante.
example_translation.ru: Тебе стоит попробовать этот новый ресторан.
example_translation.ja: この新しいレストランを試してみてください。
example_translation.ko: 이 새 식당을 한번 가 봐요.
example_translation.zh: 你应该试试这家新餐厅。

culturalContext: Trying and effort are praised in English-speaking cultures. 'Try your best,' 'nice try,' and the growth mindset encourage attempting even when failure is possible.
usageNotes: 'Try to do' (attempt) vs 'try doing' (experiment). 'Give it a try' = attempt. 'Try on' = test clothing. 'Try out' = test/audition.
funFact: Yoda's famous line 'Do or do not, there is no try' contradicts the English-speaking cultural norm of valuing the attempt itself.
grammarNote: Regular verb. 'Try to do' (make an effort) vs 'try doing' (experiment with). 'Try on' = test clothes. 'Try out' = test/audition.
commonMistakes: 'Try to do' vs 'try doing' — different meanings
'Try and do' is informal for 'try to do' — avoid in formal writing
realWorldExamples: Yoda: 'Do or do not, there is no try.'
Common encouragement: 'Just try your best!'
Aaliyah: 'Try Again'

example_sentence: You can choose any color you want.

example_translation.es: Puedes elegir cualquier color que quieras.
example_translation.de: Du kannst jede Farbe wählen, die du möchtest.
example_translation.fr: Tu peux choisir la couleur que tu veux.
example_translation.pt: Você pode escolher qualquer cor que quiser.
example_translation.it: Puoi scegliere qualsiasi colore tu voglia.
